The correction terms were identified by global optimization against measured isometric torque. Three goodness-of-fit (GoF) objectives were evaluated over the tested knee angles: root mean square error (RMSE), fraction of variance unexplained (FVU), and maximum absolute residual. RMSE summarizes the overall error magnitude. FVU divides the sum of squared residuals by the sum of squared deviations of the measured torque from its mean, expressing the error relative to the torque variation in that test. The maximum absolute residual records the largest pointwise error. RMSE and maximum residual have torque units, whereas FVU is dimensionless; smaller values indicate closer agreement for all three.

Together, these measures assess agreement in torque magnitude and variation across the range of motion. Offsets, amplitude differences, and shifts along the knee-angle axis can affect several metrics at once, so the metrics are interpreted jointly rather than assigning each one to a single type of disagreement. Across tests with different torque ranges, the absolute and variance-normalized errors also weight the tests differently. Multiobjective optimization retains these comparisons alongside the largest local error, making the trade-offs visible instead of allowing a favorable average score to conceal a poor fit elsewhere. The resulting Pareto front contains alternative compromises among the objectives, from which the adopted terms are selected using held-out validation.
reason: Explain GoF jointly and the multiobjective trade-offs; retain the existing solver and selection procedure.

old:
The goodness-of-fit metrics used to judge the optimization results are the root mean square error (RMSE), the fraction of variance unexplained (FVU), and the maximum absolute residual, each computed between the measured and predicted isometric torque over the tested range of motion.

Each metric isolates a different aspect of disagreement between the two curves. RMSE reports the overall magnitude of the error and, when the curve shapes already agree, is dominated by the remaining level offset. FVU normalizes the error variance by the variance of the measured torque, making it scale-free: it asks whether the prediction reproduces the variation of the measurement rather than whether it is close in absolute units, is the complement of the Nash--Sutcliffe model efficiency \citep{nash_river_1970}, and takes values below one when the prediction outperforms the mean of the measurement itself. The maximum absolute residual is a worst-case local measure. A small shift of the predicted curve along the knee-angle axis produces large pointwise residuals where the torque gradient is steep and small residuals elsewhere, so this metric is sensitive to phase misalignment while responding only weakly to uniform level offsets.

This interpretation follows the standard decomposition of curve-comparison error into offset, amplitude, and pattern components \citep{taylor_summarizing_2001}: the mean square error between two curves separates into the squared mean offset, an amplitude mismatch, and a residual shape term. An equivalent three-term formulation, splitting waveform similarity into offset, amplitude, and shape, underlies the linear fit method developed for clinical gait waveform comparison \citep{iosa_assessment_2014}. The metrics used here map onto this decomposition, with RMSE carrying the level disagreement, FVU the shape and amplitude agreement, and the maximum absolute residual serving as the phase-sensitive worst case. FVU is treated as the primary criterion because it is the only one of the three that is directly comparable across tests with different torque scales.

Three goodness-of-fit (GoF) objectives were evaluated over the tested knee angles: root mean square error (RMSE), fraction of variance unexplained (FVU), and maximum absolute residual. RMSE summarizes the overall error magnitude. FVU divides the sum of squared residuals by the sum of squared deviations of the measured torque from its mean, expressing the error relative to the torque variation in that test. The maximum absolute residual records the largest pointwise error. RMSE and maximum residual have torque units, whereas FVU is dimensionless; smaller values indicate closer agreement for all three.

Together, these measures assess agreement in torque magnitude and variation across the range of motion. Offsets, amplitude differences, and shifts along the knee-angle axis can affect several metrics at once, so the metrics are interpreted jointly rather than assigning each one to a single type of disagreement. Across tests with different torque ranges, the absolute and variance-normalized errors also weight the tests differently. Multiobjective optimization retains these comparisons alongside the largest local error, making the trade-offs visible instead of allowing a favorable average score to conceal a poor fit elsewhere. The resulting Pareto front contains alternative compromises among the objectives, from which the adopted terms are selected using held-out validation.

This joint interpretation is consistent with describing curve disagreement in terms of offset, amplitude, and pattern \citep{taylor_summarizing_2001, iosa_assessment_2014}, but none of the three GoF measures identifies one component exclusively. In particular, FVU is based on the full squared residual, including any mean offset; it is the complement of the Nash--Sutcliffe model efficiency and is below one when the prediction outperforms a constant prediction equal to the measured mean \citep{nash_river_1970}. FVU provides the variance-normalized comparison across tests, while RMSE and maximum residual retain the absolute error information needed to judge torque predictions.
reason: Replace the one-metric-per-error interpretation with a joint assessment and explicit multiobjective rationale.
